segments.t: Hi, I'm Alice, and welcome to T L D R Daily, your quick tour of today's tech news.
And I'm Michael. Today leans hard on security, with a strong thread about A I agents being attacked, and a few platform stories worth knowing.

Let's start with the one that needs action first. T L D R Information Security reports a critical authentication bypass in Xen Orchestra, the web platform used to manage X C P N G virtualization hosts.

And it's already being exploited. A remote attacker who can reach the management portal sends a specially crafted cookie, and that retrieves login tokens. From there they can run code on managed pools and take over the whole cluster.
Absolutely, that's the worst case for a management plane.
So what should people do?
Upgrade as soon as possible, and take that portal off the public internet. Management consoles should never be open to everyone.
Next, data. The same newsletter says the Japanese furniture giant Nitori disclosed that hackers stole about thirty-seven point six million customer records.
Names, emails, home addresses, phone numbers, birth dates and order details, for members, regular customers and corporate accounts. Nitori says no passwords or card numbers were taken.
Right. That still gives scammers plenty to build convincing phishing.

Then there's Grok Build. A firm called Claroc says it found more than thirty-five thousand public Grok Build apps by watching passive D N S records. The random part of each link sat in the subdomain, so D N S services logged the links.
And what leaked?
Per the report, sales plans from SpaceXSI, about thirty-seven hundred worker medical exams, Tesla technician scorecards and Navy contractor rosters.
Wow, that's a lot.

That is a lot of exposure from one newsletter. Third in this group is Railway. The hosting provider says an October attack exposed at most one hundred thousand customers' workspace environment variables.

The attacker escaped file system isolation, stole an internal credential, then used stolen source code to find a second flaw. Their goal was A I provider keys, and the newsletter says it led to about seven hundred forty thousand dollars in fraudulent A I charges. Railway says it will compensate victims it cannot refund.
Exactly, rotate any keys you stored there.
Definitely. And Fireworks A I also expanded its breach disclosure on November ninth. T L D R says hackers reached customer datasets, partial model weights and billing data.
Now the A I agent security thread. Both the InfoSec and I T newsletters cover Microsoft's research called Lazarus.

Researchers edited fewer than ten rarely used neurons in an open-weight model to hide a command. When a trigger appears in a prompt or tool output, the agent may run attacker commands with its normal permissions. They reached ninety-eight point eight percent success on one model using seven edited neurons.
Good point, because nobody reads neurons by hand.
So how do you defend?
Microsoft advises comparing checkpoints with base weights, using private model registries, sandboxing agent code, limiting network access, and requiring approval for high-impact actions.

Related, the InfoSec newsletter says an open-source A I penetration testing framework called Artex was repurposed by attackers. One group used it to send more than a hundred fifty thousand authentication requests, then stole ConnectWise credentials and hit over two thousand downstream Microsoft cloud environments.
Totally. A defensive tool, turned into a weapon.

And Depi researchers showed a prompt injection in a Git Hub issue could make a Codex workflow run shell commands and poison a build cache. It came within one maintainer action of a backdoored npm package. OpenAI fixed it before any bad release.

Two more quick security notes. Unit 42 describes Falcon, a browser-only attack framework planted through script tags in thirty-nine Roundcube webmail portals. Defenders should check templates for unfamiliar script tags.
And a lab post explains that a revoked Microsoft three sixty five session can keep working for up to ninety minutes. The only guaranteed instant cutoff is disabling the account.
Moving to I T. Anthropic announced Claude Meetings, which joins Google Meet calls, takes notes, retrieves information and drafts action plans while people are still talking.

It's in beta for Team and Enterprise customers. The I T newsletter also says new interactive connectors let you work inside Adobe, Notion, Atlassian, Salesforce and Hub Spot from within Claude. Computerworld frames it as direct competition with Microsoft and Google.
Fair point, so check what meeting data those connectors can reach.

One more point from the I T newsletter. IBM and Microsoft launched Imagine Enterprise, with six thousand prebuilt agents on Azure. But the customers still own their own regulatory duties, even when the platform supplies governance tools.
Quick-fire round. Yandex restored about ninety-seven percent of customer data after drone strikes, but the rest is lost because customers had no backups.

A C N C F post says platform engineering must serve both humans and agents, using machine-readable policy and scoped identities. And Howden says data center power demand grows about nineteen percent a year, against two percent for grid capacity.
Also, Anthropic added up to four point three billion dollars in Microsoft compute deals, and OpenAI says its Control Room kill switch halts research model output within thirty-five seconds.
Adobe also plans to let assistants like Claude edit inside Photoshop and Premiere through M C P, with a private beta in early twenty twenty-seven.
The main T L D R edition adds that Nvidia is working with an outside firm on C E O candidates, and the Gemini Decisions A P I can score up to a thousand questions in one pass.
So, our three actions for today. First, patch Xen Orchestra and close public access to any management portal.
Second, rotate A I provider keys and secrets stored in hosting platforms. Third, sandbox your A I agents and require approval for risky actions.
That's our brief. Thanks for listening. I'm Michael.
And I'm Alice. See you tomorrow.
